item.title: Gotsu Summer Fireworks: Hanabi on the Gonokawa River — Guide
item.description: The Gotsu summer fireworks festival is held on a summer evening over the broad estuary where the Gonokawa river, the longest in the Chugoku region, meets the Sea of Japan at the coastal town of Gotsu. Thousands of shells are launched over the wide water, their reflections doubling the display, in a relaxed local celebration that draws people from across the western Iwami district. Compared with the huge, packed fireworks festivals of the big cities, this is a more intimate riverside affair — food stalls, families in yukata and a small-town summer atmosphere on the banks of a great river.

item.title: Miyazaki Fireworks Festival — Guide
item.description: Summer in Miyazaki brings spectacular fireworks festivals (hanabi taikai), a beloved highlight of the Japanese summer. Miyazaki city’s display is among the largest in the region, launching thousands of fireworks over the river or coast on a warm evening and filling the night sky with brilliant bursts of colour, cascading golden willows, huge starbursts and creative choreographed sequences building to a thunderous grand finale. Held as part of the city’s summer festivities, the event draws big crowds who gather along the riverbanks, parks and viewing areas in the balmy night air, enjoying food stalls, festival treats and the electric atmosphere as they wait for the show.

item.title: Naniwa Yodogawa Fireworks: Osaka's Great Summer Hanabi — Guide
item.description: The Naniwa Yodogawa Fireworks Festival is one of the biggest and best-loved summer events in Osaka, staged on a single night in high summer over the broad Yodogawa river in the north of the city. Run largely on public donations, it sends tens of thousands of shells into the sky in a tightly choreographed programme, the wide river giving space for huge low bursts reflected in the water and a finale that fills the whole sky.

item.title: Oita Fireworks Festival — Guide
item.description: Summer in Oita brings spectacular fireworks festivals (hanabi taikai), a beloved centrepiece of the Japanese summer, and Oita city’s display is among the region’s biggest. On a warm evening, thousands of fireworks are launched over the river and city, filling the night sky with brilliant bursts of colour, cascading golden willows, huge starbursts and creative set-pieces choreographed to build to a thunderous finale, all reflected in the water below. Held as part of the city’s summer festivities, the event draws huge crowds who gather along the riverbanks and viewing areas in the warm night air, enjoying food stalls, festival treats and the electric atmosphere as they wait for the show.

item.title: Lake Biwa Fireworks: Summer Nights Over Otsu — Guide
item.description: The Lake Biwa Great Fireworks Festival, held on an evening in early August off Otsu, is one of the Kansai region’s biggest summer displays: some 10,000 shells burst over the open lake, their colours mirrored in the broad dark water and reflected off the lakeside towers of Otsu, drawing hundreds of thousands of spectators to the shore. Because the launches are over water with no obstructions, the shells hang huge and clear above the lake, and the setting — Japan’s largest lake, an easy ten minutes from Kyoto — makes it one of the most accessible major hanabi for visitors based in the old capital.

item.title: Nagoya Port Fireworks: Summer Lights Over the Harbour — Guide
item.description: The Nagoya Port Festival (Minato Matsuri), held around Marine Day in late July, is the city’s signature summer night: some 3,000 fireworks burst directly over the harbour basin, their colours mirrored in the black water and framed by the silhouettes of cranes and ships in one of Japan’s busiest working ports. Through the afternoon the Garden Pier area fills with festival dance parades, taiko drumming and rank upon rank of food stalls, so the evening builds from street-festival bustle to the concentrated spectacle of the finale barrages.

item.title: Kisarazu Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi & Access
item.description: Each summer, the bayside city of Kisarazu lights up the night with one of inner Tokyo Bay’s biggest fireworks festivals (hanabi) — a beloved August tradition that sends tens of thousands of shells bursting over the water. Held along the Kisarazu waterfront near the foot of the Aqua-Line, the display reflects spectacularly off the bay and draws huge crowds in summer yukata to picnic, snack at festival stalls and watch the sky erupt in colour.

item.title: Sumida River Fireworks Guide: Tokyo's Greatest Summer Spectacle
item.description: The Sumida River Fireworks Festival (隅田川花火大会, Sumidagawa Hanabi Taikai) is the oldest and most prestigious fireworks festival in Tokyo, with roots tracing back to 1733. Over 20,000 shells launch across two competing sites along the Sumida River on the last Saturday of July, watched by roughly one million spectators packed onto bridges, riverbanks, rooftops, and into restaurants for miles around. It is one of the definitive Tokyo summer experiences — and also one of the most logistically demanding to attend well.

item.title: Yokohama Fireworks Guide: Summer Hanabi, Spots & Access
item.description: There are few sights more magical than fireworks (hanabi) bursting over Yokohama’s Minato Mirai skyline, their colours mirrored in the bay beside the glowing Ferris wheel and illuminated towers. Summer is firework season across Japan, and Yokohama’s waterfront — with its open harbour, parks and promenades — makes one of the country’s most photogenic backdrops. From large bay-side festivals to special event displays, tens of thousands gather on warm evenings in yukata to watch the sky light up.
